clinicalPearls: Calculi within the salivary ducts or glands, most commonly affecting the submandibular gland and its duct
Classically causes recurrent, mealtime-related painful swelling of the affected gland as saliva flow is obstructed by eating
The submandibular predilection reflects its more viscous, mineral-rich secretions and the uphill course of Wharton duct
Stones may be palpable along the floor of mouth, and bimanual examination can help localise a distal calculus
Obstruction predisposes to secondary bacterial sialadenitis with a tender, erythematous gland and purulent ductal discharge
Ultrasound is a useful first-line investigation, and sialography or CT can define stones and duct anatomy, while sialendoscopy allows both diagnosis and treatment
Management ranges from conservative measures (hydration, sialogogues, gland massage, warm compresses) to sialendoscopy or duct stone removal, with gland excision reserved for refractory disease
Gland-preserving techniques such as sialendoscopy and transoral stone retrieval have reduced the need for gland removal
reference.pathophysiology: Sialolithiasis develops when calcium phosphate and other salts deposit around an organic nidus within a salivary duct or gland, gradually forming a calculus. Stasis of saliva, changes in its composition, ductal inflammation and dehydration favour stone formation. The submandibular gland is most often affected because its saliva is more viscous and alkaline and its duct runs upward against gravity with a relatively narrow orifice. An obstructing stone impedes salivary outflow, producing the characteristic painful mealtime swelling, and the resulting stasis predisposes to ascending bacterial infection and, over time, chronic gland damage and fibrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Acute bacterial or viral sialadenitis without a stone
Salivary gland tumour, benign or malignant
Sjogren syndrome and other autoimmune sialadenitis
additionalInvestigations: Ultrasound of the salivary gland and duct as a first-line test
Non-contrast CT to detect and localise calculi
Sialography or MR sialography to define ductal anatomy and strictures
Microbiological culture of ductal discharge when infection is present
redFlags: Features of acute suppurative sialadenitis with systemic sepsis or spreading floor-of-mouth infection
A firm, fixed or rapidly enlarging gland mass suggesting neoplasm rather than a stone
Facial nerve weakness, which is not expected with benign stone disease and suggests malignancy
Airway compromise from significant floor-of-mouth swelling or abscess
reference.prognosis: Most cases resolve with conservative measures or minimally invasive gland-preserving stone removal, and outcomes are generally good. Recurrent obstruction and chronic infection can cause irreversible gland damage, occasionally requiring gland excision.
pitfalls: Assuming all obstructive gland swelling is due to a stone and missing an underlying tumour
Overlooking secondary infection that requires antimicrobial treatment and drainage
Proceeding to gland excision before trying gland-preserving techniques
Failing to recognise multiple or proximal stones that alter the treatment approach

management: Conservative measures to promote spontaneous stone passage, including hydration, sialogogues, gland massage and warm compresses
Gland-preserving stone removal by sialendoscopy, intraoral duct incision or extracorporeal and intracorporeal lithotripsy for larger calculi
Antibiotics for secondary bacterial sialadenitis together with analgesia for pain and swelling
Sialadenectomy reserved for recurrent obstruction or irreversible gland damage
Ultrasound as first-line imaging, with CT or sialography to localise stones and define ductal anatomy for treatment planning
Advice on hydration and salivary stimulation to reduce recurrence
